- C006 (inference): Main technical risk: elapsed-time decay is not the legal validity relation; monotone proximity to query date can select a version not in force, and Prior et al.'s result suggests hard interval filtering dominates.
- C007 (inference): Main experimental confounder: temporal weight λ and the query-date distribution; a soft temporal term tuned on a benchmark whose queries are date-anchored can improve accuracy simply by upweighting whatever version the benchmark's gold passage came from (label leakage via timestamp), and recency bias vs historical anchoring trade-off means aggregate accuracy can mask opposite per-regime effects. Also, LLM-as-judge.
- C008 (assumption): the assumption that version timestamps available/reliable — record as assumption claim.
- C009 (evidence): Prior et al. dataset is only 312 QA pairs, German only. Quote? "we present a benchmark of 312 expert-validated, time-sensitive German statutory QA pairs spanning three categories". direct evidence for limited scale/generalization.
- C010 (evidence): health paper quote that favoring recent docs improves macro F1 up to 10% — direct, showing recency as a benefit in another domain (confounder: recency vs date-conditional).
- C011 (inference): evaluation gap — no retrieved work reports retrieval-layer version-selection accuracy for legal amendment retrieval; Prior et al. don't report retrieval ranking metrics, so the idea's claimed retrieval-agnostic improvement lacks a comparison point.

input.strongest_for: The problem is real and documented: amendment-driven post-cutoff staleness and recency bias cause severe degradation in statutory QA, and retrieving the version valid at the query date substantially improves answers (C002, C004; arxiv:2605.23497). A training-free temporal re-ranking component is demonstrably effective in another domain (up to +74%; C001; arxiv:2401.13222), and no retrieved work reports retrieval-layer version-selection accuracy for legal amendment retrieval (C007), so a careful, per-regime domain study with an explicit soft-versus-hard comparison would address a genuine measurement gap even if the mechanism is not new.
input.strongest_against: The core mechanism is pre-empted: TempRALM already adds an elapsed-time temporal term to a retriever's semantic score, is explicitly retrieval-agnostic, and needs no re-indexing (C001, C005; arxiv:2401.13222), and it already masks future-dated passages (C003), which is the 'not-yet-in-force' half of the problem. In the target legal setting, the strongest retrieved evidence concludes that temporal validity must be a hard constraint and that the retrieved timeframe matters more than the retrieval method (C002, C010; arxiv:2605.23497). Combined with the fact that monotone elapsed-time proximity is not the legal validity relation (C008, C010), the headline hypothesis is arguably contradicted by the nearest legal evidence, leaving only an implementation-level and domain-transfer difference.
input.most_important_unresolved_question: Can a soft elapsed-time temporal term beat, complement, or at least not harm hard version/validity-interval filtering on the same amended-regulatory corpus, retriever and query set - measured by version-selection accuracy and answer accuracy - when the temporal weight lambda is tuned without access to gold-version labels (U004, U007)?
input.most_dangerous_confounder: Gold-version label leakage through the timestamp: every benchmark question is date-anchored near a specific gold version, so a monotone timestamp term gives a shortcut that lambda tuning can exploit, inflating accuracy without temporal reasoning; aggregate metrics over current and historical regimes can further mask opposite effects (C011; arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295).
input.closest_work_explanation: arxiv:2401.13222 (TempRALM) is the closest by mechanism: semantic score plus elapsed-time temporal score, retrieval-agnostic, no re-indexing (method overlap 0.95). arxiv:2605.23497 is the closest by problem and evaluation: time-sensitive statutory QA over amended provisions with an as-of-date version filter, a 312-item benchmark and LLM-as-judge scoring (problem overlap 0.95, evaluation overlap 0.85). doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097 (TaxFlow) is the closest deployed legal system, applying temporal validity filtering over amended Indian tax law (problem overlap 0.9).
input.potential_contribution: Not the mechanism. Remaining defensible contributions: (1) a head-to-head evaluation of soft elapsed-time re-ranking versus hard validity-interval filtering (and interval-aware hybrid variants) on identical corpora, retrievers and queries, reported per query-date regime with a leakage-free tuning protocol; (2) a clause-level benchmark of partially overlapping successive revisions with per-passage version timestamps and retrieval-layer version-selection metrics, which no retrieved resource provides (C004, C007; arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.1145/3589335.3651895); (3) cross-retriever validation of the wrapper (BM25 plus several dense encoders) under matched budgets, testing TempRALM's untested retrieval-agnosticism claim.
input.overlap_summary: Problem overlap is very high with statutory/legal temporal QA (arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097) and high with temporally versioned open-domain QA (arxiv:2401.13222, doi:10.1145/3589335.3651895). Method overlap is very high with TempRALM (0.95) because the proposed score = semantic similarity + elapsed-time temporal term, added without re-indexing, is its published formulation (C001, C005). Evaluation overlap is high with arxiv:2605.23497 (0.85) for the statutory setting and moderate with TIQ-style benchmarks (0.45).
input.distinction_summary: Genuine distinctions are narrow: (a) the target setting is amended statutes with dense overlap across successive versions, whereas TempRALM targets web/Wikipedia versions and TIQ targets implicit-time multi-source snippets; (b) the framing is selecting the version in force at the query date, not the most recent version, and includes historically anchored queries that expose recency bias; (c) the claimed contribution includes a clause-level overlapping-revision benchmark and cross-retriever validation that the retrieved work does not provide. However, (b) is not realized by a monotone elapsed-time term (C008, C010), so the distinction is currently aspirational rather than realized by the proposed mechanism.
input.status_rationale: The central mechanism is already published (TempRALM) and the target legal problem already has a benchmark and a hard-filter solution that the strongest retrieved evidence judges superior in kind. The idea's remaining novelty is domain transfer, a benchmark, and an evaluation comparison - not a new method. Because the headline hypothesis is at best unverified and at worst contradicted by the nearest legal evidence, and because a serious confounder (label leakage) could manufacture the expected gain, 'promising_needs_validation' would overstate the case. It is not 'weak_or_flawed' either: the problem is real, the evaluation gap is genuine, and a reframed contribution could still be valuable.

novelty.finding: The proposed retrieval-agnostic, training-free semantic + elapsed-time temporal scoring wrapper is essentially TempRALM's published Eq. 4-5, including its explicit claim to extend any numeric-similarity retriever without re-indexing. This is not a merely similar approach; it is the same mechanism.
novelty.question: Has essentially the same idea already been proposed?

novelty.finding: The target setting already has a benchmark and a hard-constraint solution (Prior et al., 312 German statutory QA pairs; TaxFlow for Indian tax law), so the domain transfer is into an occupied rather than empty space.
novelty.question: Is the legal/regulatory domain still an unexplored application of the mechanism?

novelty.finding: The difference between the proposed method and existing work is implementation-level (continuous soft decay versus discrete interval filtering), not conceptual. Soft proximity was already evaluated in a non-legal domain, and hard filtering was already evaluated in the legal domain; the missing piece is a controlled comparison, not a new idea.
novelty.question: Is the difference only implementation-level?

technical_validity.finding: Elapsed-time decay is monotone in |t_q - t_v|, but legal applicability is determined by validity intervals. A version can be temporally nearest yet not in force, and a correct old version can be far in time. The proposed signal is therefore not a valid proxy for the property being optimized (which version governs the query date).
technical_validity.question: Is the proposed mechanism technically valid for its stated legal goal?

technical_validity.finding: The 'not-yet-in-force passage' failure mode the idea implicitly targets is already handled in existing work by masking future-dated passages, reducing the technical space left for a new contribution.
technical_validity.question: Which part of the stated failure mode is still unaddressed?

technical_validity.finding: The mechanism presupposes per-passage version timestamps and per-query target dates. Both are assumed, not verified: real corpora may lack clause-level timestamps and query dates may need inference, which would inject noise into the very signal being relied on.
technical_validity.question: Are the required temporal inputs available and reliable?

experimental_validity.finding: Because benchmark questions are date-anchored near their gold version, a monotone timestamp term is partially label-revealing. Tuning lambda on the same benchmark risks fitting the gold-version timestamp rather than solving retrieval, so an accuracy gain would not be evidence for the hypothesis.
experimental_validity.question: What confounder could produce the claimed result without the mechanism being responsible?

experimental_validity.finding: The comparison set must include a hard validity-interval filter and semantic-only retrieval under matched budgets, and must report retrieval-layer version-selection accuracy. No retrieved work reports such retrieval metrics for legal amendment retrieval, so a result could look novel simply because no baseline was measured.
experimental_validity.question: Are the baselines strong and are budgets matched?

experimental_validity.finding: Aggregate answer accuracy mixes current-version and historical-version questions whose expected optimal temporal weight points in opposite directions; a single aggregate number can show no effect while both regimes change substantially, or show a gain driven by one regime.
experimental_validity.question: Does the metric design hide regime-dependent effects?

experimental_validity.finding: The only version-aware statutory benchmark is 312 synthetic, LLM-generated and expert-validated German pairs. Building a new benchmark from the same recipe reproduces its construct-validity weakness, and its size limits statistical power for per-regime analysis.
experimental_validity.question: Is the planned benchmark's construct valid enough to support the claim?

practicality.finding: The wrapper is genuinely cheap: it adds a scalar term to existing scores, needs no retraining or re-indexing, and is therefore easy to deploy and to port across retrievers.
practicality.question: Is the approach practically feasible and attractive to adopt?

practicality.finding: If hard version filtering already solves the legal case and is simpler to reason about and audit, a tune-one-hyperparameter soft score offers little practical advantage; practitioners with reliable validity metadata would choose the filter, and those without it cannot compute either.
practicality.question: Which method would a practitioner actually deploy?

practicality.finding: Deployment at scale depends on clause-level version metadata and reliable date extraction, both of which are assumed here and only demonstrated by a regex extractor in one jurisdiction.
practicality.question: What does deployment require beyond the ranking change?

input.resolution: Resolved against the elapsed-time proxy. TempRALM's temporal score is monotone in the query-document time difference (C008; arxiv:2401.13222), whereas Prior et al. derive legal applicability from effective/amendment dates and conclude that temporal validity must be taken "as a hard constraint" (C002, C010; arxiv:2605.23497). Legal in-force status is an interval relation, so elapsed time to a version timestamp is not a valid proxy for which revision governs the query date; an interval-aware (in-force indicator or piecewise) term is required if the legal framing is kept.

input.description: Benchmark queries are date-anchored near a specific gold version, so a monotone timestamp term partially reveals the label. If the temporal weight lambda is tuned on the same benchmark that is used to report the gain, the result may reflect hyperparameter fitting to gold-version timestamps rather than genuine temporal relevance. This is the single most dangerous way the expected improvement could be manufactured.
input.question: Could the expected accuracy gain from the soft temporal term be an artifact of tuning lambda against gold-version-anchored questions (timestamp label leakage), rather than evidence of genuine temporal ranking skill?
input.rationale: If this confounder is not excluded by design (held-out tuning, timestamp-shuffled control, no-timestamp baseline), a positive result would not support the hypothesis and the whole contribution would be undermined.

input.description: The idea claims retrieval-agnosticism, but TempRALM instantiates a single retriever (Atlas/Contriever) and no retrieved work evaluates a temporal re-ranking wrapper across multiple sparse and dense retrievers under matched budgets. It is unknown whether the soft temporal term's effect is stable across retrievers or is an artifact of one embedding space, chunking scheme and top-k.
input.question: Does a soft temporal re-ranking term behave consistently across different retriever families (BM25 and several dense encoders) and top-k budgets, or is any gain specific to one retriever configuration?
input.rationale: Retrieval-agnosticism is a headline claim of the idea; without cross-retriever evidence under matched budgets the claim is unsupported even if one configuration improves.
